ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 3 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Judy Garland — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Four-week review eleven days after a supervised hospital change from secobarbital to phenobarbital: starting the outpatient taper and the stimulant taper

text.paragraph: Four-week review, eleven days after the supervised change to phenobarbital. [S]

Ms. Garland returns eleven days after a four-day admission to the addiction medicine service. Secobarbital was stopped on admission and phenobarbital was started and adjusted with withdrawal scoring; she had a mild tremor and poor sleep on the second night, no seizure and no confusion, and she was discharged on phenobarbital 32.4 mg three times daily. She has taken it as prescribed from the one-week supply and has taken no secobarbital. She was drowsy for the first three days at home, and that has passed. She sleeps four to five hours a night; her sleep diary shows that she lies awake for an hour after late rehearsals. She has kept to one 10 mg dextroamphetamine tablet each morning. She has taken sertraline 50 mg daily without side effects. Her mood is a little better. The dietitian could not see her yet because of a waiting list. [S]

Barbiturate use disorder on phenobarbital (F13.20). Stable on 97.2 mg a day with no withdrawal and no sedation, so the outpatient taper can begin. Urine test shows barbiturates, as expected on phenobarbital, and amphetamine. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or self-harm; supply locked away. [S]
Phenobarbital 16.2 mg tablets on the written taper schedule: 81 mg a day from today (32.4 mg morning, 16.2 mg afternoon, 32.4 mg at bedtime), then 64.8 mg a day in two weeks if she is well, with a nurse phone check before each step.
Dispensed two weeks at a time.
Call the same day for tremor, sweating, confusion or a seizure.

Stimulant use disorder (prescribed amphetamine), mild (F15.10). Barbiturate now stable, so the stimulant taper starts as planned. [S]
Dextroamphetamine 5 mg each morning for two weeks, then stop.
Expect tiredness and more sleep for a week or two; regular meals and daylight walks help.

Chronic insomnia (G47.00). Sleep short, as expected early in the taper. CBT-I has begun. [S]
A fixed wake time, a wind-down hour after late rehearsals, and out of bed when unable to sleep; sleep restriction to wait until the taper is further along.

Depression with anxious distress on sertraline (F32.1). PHQ-9 12 from 14, GAD-7 11 from 13; early improvement three weeks after reaching 50 mg. [S]
Continue sertraline 50 mg daily and weekly psychotherapy.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering: Considerations When Risks Outweigh Benefits (2025); The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020); The ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder (2024); Clinical Practice Guideline for the Pharmacologic Treatment of Chronic Insomnia in Adults: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline (2017); Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2016); U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024 (2024); Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) (2026); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026)

Follow-up: Nurse phone check before each taper step. Ten-week review in six weeks. Weekly psychotherapy and CBT-I. Next scheduled visit 1955-08-31: ten-week review: phenobarbital taper, life after stopping the stimulant, sleep, mood, weight and work. [S]
